{{Short description|Mass dancing mania in Strasbourg}}
The '''dancing plague of 1518''', or '''dance epidemic of 1518''' ({{Langx|fr|Épidémie dansante de 1518}}; {{Langx|de|Straßburger Tanzwut}}), was a case of [[dancing mania]] that occurred in [[Strasbourg]], [[Alsace]] (modern-day [[France]]), in the [[Holy Roman Empire]] from July 1518 to September 1518. Somewhere between 50 and 400 people took to dancing for weeks. There are many theories behind the phenomenon, the most popular being stress-induced [[mass hysteria]], suggested by John Waller.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Viegas |first=Jennifer |date=August 1, 2008 |title='Dancing Plague' and Other Odd Afflictions Explained : Discovery News |url=http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2008/08/01/dancing-death-mystery.html |archive-date=October 13, 2012 |access-date=2023-04-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121013075434/http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2008/08/01/dancing-death-mystery.html }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Waller |first=John |date=February 2009 |title=A forgotten plague: making sense of dancing mania |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S014067360960386X |journal=The Lancet |language=en |volume=373 |issue=9664 |pages=624–625 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(09)60386-X |pmid=19238695|s2cid=35094677 }}</ref> Other theories include [[ergot poisoning]]. There is controversy concerning the number of deaths.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Pennant-Rea |first=Ned |date=July 10, 2018 |title=The Dancing Plague of 1518 |url=https://publicdomainreview.org/essay/the-dancing-plague-of-1518/ |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=The Public Domain Review |language=en}}</ref>

== History ==
=== Events ===
The outbreak began in July 1518 when a woman known as Frau Troffea and her daughter Fräulein Emma Götz began to dance fervently and uncontrollably in a street in Strasbourg. According to Ned Pennant-Rea, "Frau Troffea had started dancing on July 14th on the narrow cobbled street outside her [[half-timbered]] home. As far as we can tell she had no musical accompaniment but simply 'began to dance' ... some of those who had witnessed her strange performance had begun to mimic her, and within days more than thirty [[choreomaniacs]] were in motion, some so [[monomania]]cally that only death would have the power to intervene."<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":0" /> Troffea kept up the constant dancing for a week. Soon, three dozen others joined in.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Andrews |first=Evan |date=August 31, 2015 |title=What was the dancing plague of 1518? |url=https://www.history.com/news/what-was-the-dancing-plague-of-1518 |access-date=2023-05-02 |website=HISTORY |publisher=A&E Television Networks |language=en}}</ref> This is known and believed by some to be a perfect example of a [[nocebo effect]] which can make some feel ill simply by being under the expectation of being ill. By August, the "dancing plague" had claimed 400 victims.<ref name=":5" /> Dancers were beginning to collapse. It is said some even died from a stroke or heart attack.<ref name=":5" /> The victims' movements were described as [[spasm]]atic with many convulsions and their bodies were left drenched in sweat. Their arms would thrash violently and some noted that their eyes were vacant and expressionless. Blood would pool into their swollen feet and they would eventually bleed into their shoes. Often, there would also be cries for help from the affected. If the victims did not succumb to a heart attack, they would collapse from extreme exhaustion, hunger, and thirst. There were as many as 15 deaths per day during the outbreak’s peak, but the final number of fatalities is unknown today.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Waller |first1=John |title=A Time to dance, a time to die: The extraordinary story of the dancing plague of 1518 |date=January 1, 2008 |publisher=Icon |location=London, England |edition=1 |url=https://www.iconbooks.com/ib-title/a-time-to-dance-a-time-to-die/ |access-date=2023-10-20}}</ref>  No one knew what caused this reaction, which meant no one understood how to remedy it. By early September, the outbreak began to subside.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Bauer |first=Patricia |title=Dancing plague of 1518 {{!}} Facts & Theories {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/event/dancing-plague-of-1518 |access-date=2023-04-24 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5" />

Historical documents, including "physician notes, cathedral sermons, local and regional chronicles, and even notes issued by the Strasbourg city council" are clear that the victims danced;<ref name=":0" /> it is not known why. Historical sources agree that there was an outbreak of dancing after a single woman started dancing,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Midelfort |first=H. C. Erik |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9WXkw2K8O8YC&pg=PA33 |title=A History of Madness in Sixteenth-Century Germany |date=1999 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-4169-9 |language=en}}</ref> and the dancing did not seem to die down. It lasted for such a long time that it even attracted the attention of the authorities; until the council gave up authority to the physicians, who prescribed the afflicted to "dance themselves free of it."<ref name=":4" /> There are claims that guild halls were refurbished to accommodate the dancing, as well as musicians and strong people to help keep those dealing with the dancing mania to stay upright.<ref name=":4" /> This backfired, and the council was forced to ban public dancing as people danced in fear it was a punishment from [[Saint Vitus]]; and to be "free of sin" many joined in on the dancing epidemic.<ref name=":4" /> When divine punishment or demonic possession initiated and sustained frenzied dancing, only those with divinely bestowed authority could restore the sinners to wholeness and to a right relationship with the divine.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Miller |first=Lynneth J. |date=2017-11-01 |title=Divine Punishment or Disease? Medieval and Early Modern Approaches to the 1518 Strasbourg Dancing Plague |url=https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/full/10.3366/drs.2017.0199 |journal=Dance Research |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=149–164 |doi=10.3366/drs.2017.0199 |issn=0264-2875|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The council went as far as to ban music, as well.<ref name=":4" /> Those who danced were then ordered to go to the shrine of Saint Vitus believed to punish sinners by compelling them to dance uncontrollably,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wright |first1=Jennifer |title=Get Well Soon History's Worst Plagues and the Heroes Who Fought Them |date=February 7, 2017 |publisher=Henry Holt and Company |isbn=978-1627797467 |pages=56–58 }}</ref> wore red shoes that were sprinkled with holy water and had painted crosses on the tops and soles.<ref name=":4" /> They also had to hold small crosses in their hands; and incense and Latin incantations were part of this "ritual."<ref name=":4" /> Apparently "forgiven by Vitus," word was spread of a successful ritual and the Dancing Plague had ended in September when the remaining dancers were taken to a mountaintop to pray for absolution.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Andrews |first1=Evan |title=What Was the Dancing Plague of 1518? |url=https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-dancing-plague-of-1518 |website=History.com |date=31 August 2015 |publisher=A&E Television Networks. |access-date=April 17, 2025}}</ref><ref name=":4" />

Events similar to this are said to have occurred throughout the medieval age including 11th century in [[Ilberstedt|Cölbigk]], [[Saxony]], where it was believed to be the result of divine judgment.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Miller |first=Lynneth J. |date=November 2017 |title=Divine Punishment or Disease? Medieval and Early Modern Approaches to the 1518 Strasbourg Dancing Plague |url=https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/drs.2017.0199 |journal=Dance Research |language=en |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=149–164 |doi=10.3366/drs.2017.0199 |issn=0264-2875 |jstor=90020124|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 15th century [[Apulia]], Italy,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Soth |first=Amelia |date=2019-01-10 |title=When Dancing Plagues Struck Medieval Europe |url=https://daily.jstor.org/when-dancing-plagues-struck-medieval-europe/ |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=JSTOR Daily |language=en-US}}</ref> a woman was bitten by a tarantula, the venom making her dance convulsively. The only way to cure the bite was to "shimmy" and to have the right sort of music available, which was an accepted remedy by scholars like [[Athanasius Kircher]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gloyne |first=Howard F. |date=March 7, 1950 |title=Tarantism; mass hysterical reaction to spider bite in the Middle Ages |journal=The American Imago; A Psychoanalytic Journal for the Arts and Sciences |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=29–42 |issn=0065-860X |jstor=26301236 |pmid=15413592}}</ref>

Contemporaneous explanations included [[demonic possession]] and overheated blood.<ref name=":1" />

==Veracity of deaths==
Controversy exists over whether people ultimately danced to death. Some sources claim that for a period the plague killed around fifteen people per day,<ref name=":3"/> but the sources of the city of Strasbourg at the time of the events did not mention the number of deaths, or even if there were fatalities. There do not appear to be any sources related to the events that make note of any fatalities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Clementz |first=Élisabeth |date=2016-10-01 |title=Waller (John), Les danseurs fous de Strasbourg. Une épidémie de transe collective en 1518 |journal=Revue d'Alsace |volume=142 |language=fr |issue=142 |pages=451–453 |doi=10.4000/alsace.2457 |issn=0181-0448|doi-access=free }}</ref> Ned Pennant-Rea also claims that the final death toll is not known, but if the claims of fifteen people dying per day were true then the toll could be "into the hundreds".<ref name=":4"/>

The main source for the claim is John Waller, who has written several journal articles on the subject and the book ''A Time to Dance, a Time to Die: The Extraordinary Story of the Dancing Plague of 1518''. The sources cited by Waller that mention deaths were all from later accounts of the events. There is also uncertainty around the identity of the initial dancer (either an unnamed woman or "Frau Troffea") and the number of dancers involved (somewhere between 50 and 400). Of the six chronicle accounts, four support Lady Troffea as the first dancer.<ref name=":2"/>

==Modern theories==
=== Food poisoning ===
Some believe<ref name=":1"/> the dancing could have been brought on by food poisoning caused by the toxic and psychoactive chemical products of [[ergot]] fungi ([[ergotism]]), which grows commonly on grains (such as rye) used for baking bread. [[Ergotamine]] is the main psychoactive product of ergot fungi; it is structurally related to the drug [[lysergic acid diethylamide]] (LSD-25) and is the substance from which LSD-25 was originally synthesized. The same fungus has also been implicated in other major historical anomalies, including the [[Salem witch trials]].<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2014-06-04 |title=The Witches Curse ~ Clues and Evidence {{!}} Secrets of the Dead |url=https://www.pbs.org/wnet/secrets/witches-curse-clues-evidence/1501/ |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=Secrets of the Dead |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Fessenden |first=Maris |date=June 24, 2016 |title=A Strange Case of Dancing Mania Struck Germany Six Centuries Ago Today |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/strange-case-dancing-mania-struck-germany-six-centuries-ago-today-180959549/ |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

In ''[[The Lancet]]'', John Waller argues that "this theory does not seem tenable, since it is unlikely that those poisoned by ergot could have danced for days at a time. Nor would so many people have reacted to its psychotropic chemicals in the same way. The ergotism theory also fails to explain why almost every outbreak occurred somewhere along the [[Rhine]] and [[Moselle]] rivers, areas linked by water but with quite different climates and crops."<ref name=":3"/>

=== Stress-induced mass hysteria ===
This could have been an example of fully developed cases of [[Functional neurologic disorder|psychogenic movement disorder]] happening in mass hysteria or [[mass psychogenic illness]], which involves many individuals suddenly exhibiting the same bizarre behavior. The behavior spreads rapidly and broadly in an epidemic pattern.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kaufman |first1=David Myland |title=Kaufman's clinical neurology for psychiatrists. Chapter 18: Involuntary Movement Disorders |last2=Milstein |first2=Mark J |date=2013 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-1-4557-4004-8 |edition=Seventh |location=London |pages=397–453 |oclc=830038162}}</ref> This kind of comportment could have been caused by elevated levels of [[psychological stress]], caused by the ruthless years (even by the rough standards of the early modern period) the people of [[Alsace]] were suffering.<ref name=":3" />

Waller speculates that the dancing was "stress-induced [[psychosis]]" on a mass level, since the region where the people danced was riddled with starvation and disease, and the inhabitants tended to be superstitious. Seven other cases of [[dancing plague]] were reported in the same region during the [[medieval era]].<ref name=":0"/>

This psychogenic illness could have created a [[chorea]] (from the Greek ''khoreia'' meaning "to dance"), a situation comprising random and intricate unintentional movements that flit from body part to body part. Diverse choreas ([[Dancing mania|St. Vitus' dance, St. John's dance]], and [[tarantism]]) were labeled in the Middle Ages referring to the independent epidemics of "dancing mania" that happened in central Europe, particularly at the time of the plague.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cardoso |first1=Francisco |last2=Seppi |first2=Klaus |last3=Mair |first3=Katherina J |last4=Wenning |first4=Gregor K |last5=Poewe |first5=Werner |date=July 2006 |title=Seminar on choreas |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S147444220670494X |journal=The Lancet Neurology |language=en |volume=5 |issue=7 |pages=589–602 |doi=10.1016/S1474-4422(06)70494-X |pmid=16781989|s2cid=41265524 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Winn |first=H. Richard |title=Youmans and Winn neurological surgery: Clinical Overview of Movement Disorders |date=2017 |isbn=978-0-323-28782-1 |edition=Seventh |location=Philadelphia, PA |pages=573–585.e7 |oclc=956520317}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kaufman |first1=David Myland |title=Kaufman's clinical neurology for psychiatrists: Involuntary Movement Disorders |last2=Geyer |first2=Howard L. |last3=Milstein |first3=Mark J. |date=2017 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-323-46131-3 |edition=Eighth |pages=389–447 |oclc=962453512}}</ref>

==Pop culture and media==
{{In popular culture|section|date=October 2025}}
This event was referenced in the 2016 ''[[The 39 Clues]]'' book, ''Superspecial: Outbreak'' by C. Alexander London.

The event inspired [[Jonathan Glazer]]'s 2020 short film ''Strasbourg 1518''.<ref>{{cite news|last=Crompton|first=Sarah|title=Strasbourg 1518: reliving a 16th-century 'dancing plague' in lockdown|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|date=2020-07-19|url=https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2020/jul/19/strasbourg-1518-reliving-16th-century-dancing-plague-in-lockdown-artangel-jonathan-glazer-sadlers-wells-bbc|access-date=2024-01-29}}</ref>

It was the inspiration behind the 2022 choral song "Choreomania" by [[Florence and the Machine]]. It was the third track on the album ''[[Dance Fever (album)|Dance Fever]]'', which took its title from the song.<ref>{{cite web|date=15 May 2022|title=On 'Dance Fever,' Florence + the Machine explores her fractured desires|url=https://www.npr.org/2022/05/15/1099021095/on-dance-fever-florence-the-machine-explores-her-fractured-desires|author1=Michel Martin|author2=Kira Wakeam|author3=Cat Sposato|work=NPR}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.songfacts.com/facts/florence-the-machine/choreomania|title=Choreomania by Florence + the Machine - Songfacts}}</ref>

The event is the subject of the graphic novel ''The Dancing Plague'' by Gareth Brookes, published by [[SelfMadeHero]] in 2021.

[[Kiran Millwood Hargrave]]'s 2022 novel ''The Dance Tree'' also discusses the events.

The book series ''A Collection of Utter Speculation'' released a title ''The Dancing Plague: A Collection of Utter Speculation'' in 2022. It is a fictional account of the events that happened in Strasbourg.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Byrne |first1=JD |last2=Guilt |first2=Elizabeth |last3=Gregory |first3=Joscelyn |last4=Henley |first4=Deborah |last5=Loftus |first5=C. Owen |last6=Rossman |first6=Jennifer Lee |last7=Thurman |first7=Allison |last8=Updike |first8=David L. |last9=Wenzel |first9=Romy Tara |date=October 2022 |title=The Dancing Plague is coming. A new Collection of Utter Speculation |url=https://lcwallingham.com/2022/09/12/the-dancing-plague-is-coming-a-new-collection-of-utter-speculation/ |access-date=2023-05-01 |website=LCW Allingham |language=en}}</ref>

The event is referenced in the 2024 song "RATKING 1518", in both title and lyrics, created by rap duo Grim Salvo.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Grim Salvo - RATKING 1518 Lyrics |url=https://genius.com/Grim-salvo-ratking-1518-lyrics}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Grim Salvo - YouTube |website=[[YouTube]] |url=https://www.youtube.com/@GrimSalvo}}</ref>

This event inspired the music video short-film for [[Loreen]] and [[Ólafur Arnalds]] joint 2025 release of their songs "In The Sound of Breathing" and "Opening" under the name "SAGES".<ref>{{Cite web |title=SAGES - by Ólafur Arnalds & Loreen | website=[[YouTube]] | date=7 March 2025 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4OTd2qBH6jQ}}</ref>

This event is discussed on the podcast The Magnus archives, in the extra episode "What The Ghost", by Sasha Sienna

Comedian [[Mae Martin]] discussed the dance plague on Pretty Little Episode #61 of the handsome podcast, it was brought it up again in the next full episode with question asker [[Lukas Gage]]. The dancing plague is considered and known as a Mae fact.<ref>{{cite web | title=Spotify | website=[[Spotify]] | url=https://open.spotify.com/episode/76fwUJEYmEDsPNgd6krMEF?si=ce48d7460d274bc7 }}</ref>

The event is the subject of the song "Died of Dancing", by Australian progressive rock band [[Toehider]]. The song directly references "Mrs. Troffea" and "hot blood" in the lyrics.<ref>{{Citation |title=Toehider – Died of Dancing |url=https://genius.com/Toehider-died-of-dancing-lyrics |access-date=2025-12-17}}</ref>
